title: MCP 2026 Specification: Stateless Core & Enterprise Auth
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol steering group shipped a new specification — the largest revision to MCP since its November 2024 launch. Where earlier versions of MCP assumed a stateful session between client and server, the 2026 spec redesigns the protocol core to be **stateless**, so servers can run on ordinary HTTP infrastructure (load balancers, serverless functions, horizontal auto-scaling) instead of requiring sticky sessions or long-lived connections.

---

## Stateless Core

The headline change is that the protocol layer no longer requires a server to remember client state between requests. Previously, an MCP server backed by a stdio or SSE transport typically held session state in process memory, which made it awkward to scale horizontally or deploy behind a standard load balancer. Under the 2026 spec, state that must persist (like an in-progress multi-step operation) is represented explicitly through protocol constructs rather than implied by a long-lived connection.

This matters most for hosted, multi-tenant MCP servers — a provider can now run MCP endpoints the same way it runs any other stateless HTTP API, and scale them with standard web infrastructure.

---

## New Extensions

**MCP Apps** — lets a server render its own UI back to the client, instead of the client having to build a generic renderer for every tool's output. This enables richer, server-defined interactive experiences (forms, visualizations, custom widgets) inside an MCP-compatible host like Claude Code or Claude Desktop.

**Tasks extension** — formalizes long-running work. Rather than holding a request open while a slow operation completes, a server can return a task handle immediately and the client polls or subscribes for completion, which fits naturally with the new stateless core.

**Authorization realignment** — MCP's auth model now tracks OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect more closely, reducing the amount of MCP-specific auth code that clients and servers each had to implement.

---

## Enterprise-Managed Authorization

A related extension, **Enterprise-Managed Authorization**, reached stable status alongside the July spec release. It lets an organization centrally provision which MCP servers its users can access through the org's existing identity provider (IdP), so a new employee gets connected servers automatically on first login rather than clicking through a separate OAuth consent screen for every app. Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta are among the adopters, alongside a growing list of MCP servers that support the flow.

This addresses a real pain point from MCP's first two years: per-app OAuth consent doesn't scale when an enterprise wants to roll out dozens of MCP servers to thousands of employees.

---

## Real-World Adoption

MCP's server ecosystem, a few hundred servers in mid-2025, has grown substantially by mid-2026:

- **Healthcare:** Florence Healthcare rolled out MCP access across its site-workflow product suite — eleven specialized tools spanning a network of roughly 65,000 clinical research sites and 30,000 active research protocols — letting agents interact natively with trial-management workflows.
- **Test automation:** Platforms including Cypress, BrowserStack, and Maestro shipped MCP servers in 2026, wiring their real testing infrastructure into coding agents rather than requiring agents to shell out to CLI wrappers.

---

## Roadmap

The published MCP roadmap includes unifying transports around **HTTP over stdio** — using HTTP/2 semantics over a local subprocess pipe, so local (stdio) and remote (HTTP) servers can share one multiplexed transport implementation while stdio keeps its process-lifecycle and sandboxing guarantees.

---

## Why It Matters for Agent Builders

For anyone building on top of MCP (as described in [Tool Use & Agents](tool-use-and-agents)), the practical takeaways are: hosted MCP servers can now be deployed like any other stateless web service, enterprise rollouts no longer require per-user OAuth clicks when Enterprise-Managed Authorization is supported, and UI-heavy tools can render their own interface via MCP Apps instead of relying on the host to guess how to display results.
